newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine considers G7 Chernobyl offer far too low.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine considers G7 Chernobyl offer far too low.

text.p: Ukraine voiced frustation on Tuesday that the Group of Seven leading industrialised nations had pledged to give only half the amount Kiev had expected to deal with the stricken Chernobyl nuclear power plant.

The G7 leaders said at their weekend summit in Denver they would give Ukraine $300 million to fix the concrete shell, or sarcophagus, hurriedly built around the reactor after it exploded 11 years ago. Kiev had wanted $750 million.

"We had a plan which was agreed earlier with G7 experts, that they would spend at least $700 million. But somehow we got only the $300 million figure in Denver," said Sergiy Parashin, director of the Chernobyl station.

"We do not have enough money for the sarcophagus and it will be very hard to deal with problems with only $300 million," Parashin said by telephone from the station, some 150 km (85 miles) north of the capital.

The five-year plan, drawn up by Ukrainian and G7 experts, foresaw stabilisation of the sarcophagus and removal and burial of some 200 tonnes of the nuclear fuel, sand, and concrete mixture inside the walls, feared by some experts to be leaking.

"Ukraine is frustrated by the G7 statement," said Yuri Kostenko, Chernobyl's top negotiator and environment minister, in an Interfax-Ukraine news agency report. "The G7 allocated only $300 million of the $750 million that we needed."
He doubted the balance of the money would be forthcoming.
"We have doubts that some other states would be able to make contributions totalling $450 million in grants," said Kostenko, now in New York with President Leonid Kuchma.
There was no immediate comment from Western officials to the Ukrainian criticism.

Cash-strapped Ukraine, left to foot the bill in the aftermath of the Soviet-era disaster, has spent $10 million a year to maintain the crumbling structure and earlier this year abandoned plans to build another shell called Sarcophagus-2.

Kuchma, responding to G7 demands, promised on the eve of the 10th anniversary of the April 26, 1986 disaster to close the station by 2000. It was the world's worst civil nuclear accident. The G7 statement in Denver reaffirmed Chernobyl should be closed completely by 2000.

Ukraine has also linked closure with the allocation of a credit, estimated at about $1.2 billion, to complete extra reactors at the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear stations in western Ukraine to replace power lost by Chernobyl's shutdown.

Kostenko said the G7 backed allocation of a credit by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), whose board of directors is due to decide in London on June 30 whether to support the building of the new reactors.
Chernobyl produces five percent of the country's electricity and only one of four reactors is operating, causing shortages and leaving the national power grid unstable.

"We have been pinning our hopes on the West for at least five years. We are tired of all the promises," Volodymyr Shlapunov, deputy director of the Khmelnytsky plant, said by telephone. "Our final hope is the EBRD money."
Shlapunov said the station had allocated some money from its fund for completion but did not have enough to finish the reactor, more than 80 percent constructed.
